hand/random-matrix-theory.html:
Universality and the Green Function Comparison Method

The central pillar of modern random matrix theory is the universality principle: local eigenvalue statistics of large random matrices depend only on the symmetry class (β = 1, 2, 4) and not on the fine details of the entry distribution. The Green function comparison method, developed by Erdős, Yau, and collaborators, provides a rigorous pathway to prove bulk and edge universality for Wigner matrices with sub‑exponential decay. The method compares the resolvent G(z) = (H − z)⁻¹ of a general Wigner matrix H with that of a Gaussian ensemble sharing the same first two moments. By interpolating between the two ensembles via a continuous Ornstein–Uhlenbeck flow on the matrix entries, one tracks the evolution of the expectation of smooth test functions of the eigenvalues. The key estimate is a local law: with high probability, the Stieltjes transform mₙ(z) = (1/n) Tr G(z) stays close to the deterministic Stieltjes transform m_sc(z) of the semicircle law down to the optimal spectral scale η ≫ n⁻¹. This local law yields rigidity of eigenvalues — each eigenvalue λ_i deviates from its classical location γ_i by at most n⁻²ᐟ³⁺ε at the edge and n⁻¹⁺ε in the bulk. Once rigidity is established, a Green function comparison theorem shows that any smooth observable of a fixed number of eigenvalues has the same limit as in the Gaussian case. The technique extends to sample covariance matrices, deformed Wigner matrices, and sparse Erdős–Rényi graphs, provided a suitable local law holds. The method also clarifies the role of the fourth moment: for β = 1,2 the fourth moment does not affect the limiting sine‑kernel or Airy‑kernel statistics, whereas for β = 4 the symplectic structure forces a different kernel. Universality thus separates into a robust “bulk” regime governed by the sine kernel and an “edge” regime governed by the Airy kernel, both independent of the entry distribution beyond the first two moments.

Dyson Brownian Motion and Eigenvalue Dynamics

Dyson Brownian motion (DBM) furnishes a dynamical picture of eigenvalue evolution that underlies many modern proofs of universality. For an n×n Hermitian matrix H(t) whose entries perform independent Ornstein–Uhlenbeck processes, the eigenvalues λ₁(t) ≤ … ≤ λₙ(t) satisfy the system of stochastic differential equations dλ_i = (1/√n) dB_i + (1/n) Σj≠i (1/(λ_i − λ_j)) dt, where B_i are independent standard Brownian motions. The drift term encodes the logarithmic repulsion between eigenvalues; the factor 1/n reflects the scaling that keeps the empirical spectral distribution of order one. The invariant measure of this diffusion is exactly the joint eigenvalue density of the corresponding Gaussian ensemble (GOE, GUE, or GSE). DBM provides a natural interpolation: starting from any Wigner matrix H(0), the flow H(t) converges to a Gaussian ensemble as t → ∞. By choosing a short time t = n⁻¹⁺ε, the eigenvalue statistics of H(t) are already universal, while the difference between H(0) and H(t) can be controlled via the Green function comparison method. This two‑step strategy — short‑time DBM relaxation followed by comparison — yields optimal universality results down to the microscopic scale. Moreover, DBM gives a probabilistic representation of the correlation kernels: the k‑point correlation functions of the eigenvalues at time t are determinantal (for β = 2) or Pfaffian (for β = 1,4) with kernels that converge to the sine kernel in the bulk and the Airy kernel at the edge. The DBM framework also extends to non‑Hermitian matrices, where the eigenvalues perform a two‑dimensional Coulomb gas dynamics, and to the singular values of rectangular matrices, leading to the Laguerre process. The stochastic differential equation perspective clarifies why eigenvalue repulsion is universal: it is a consequence of the logarithmic interaction that appears whenever the joint density contains a Vandermonde factor ∏i<j</sub> |λ_i − λ_j|^β.

Worked Example: Local Law Scale
Consider an n×n Wigner matrix with sub‑gaussian entries. State the optimal scale η for which the local semicircle law holds with high probability, and explain why this scale is sufficient to prove bulk universality via the Green function comparison method.
The optimal scale is η ≫ n⁻¹ (more precisely η ≥ n⁻¹⁺ε for any ε > 0). At this scale the Stieltjes transform mₙ(z) with Im z = η approximates the deterministic m_sc(z) with error O((nη)⁻¹). This precision yields eigenvalue rigidity: each eigenvalue λ_i deviates from its classical location γ_i by at most n⁻¹⁺ε in the bulk. Rigidity ensures that any smooth test function of a fixed number of eigenvalues depends only on the local statistics at scale n⁻¹. The Green function comparison theorem then shows that the expectation of such observables matches the Gaussian ensemble, because the interpolation flow only requires control of the resolvent down to the same scale. Hence bulk universality follows.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the “optimal scale” or “local law”, recall the hierarchy: global law (η ∼ 1), mesoscopic (η ≫ n⁻¹ᐟ²), microscopic (η ≫ n⁻¹). The microscopic scale is the threshold for universality proofs. Memorise the rigidity bound |λ_i − γ_i| ≤ n⁻¹⁺ε (bulk) and n⁻²ᐟ³⁺ε (edge). These exponents appear repeatedly in multiple‑choice and short‑answer items.

Spiked Models and the BBP Phase Transition in Detail

Spiked models describe a low‑rank perturbation of a large random matrix: H = M + Σk=1^r θ_k u_k u_k^T, where M belongs to a Gaussian ensemble and the spikes θ_k represent signal strengths. The Baik–Ben Arous–Péché (BBP) transition identifies a critical threshold θ_c = 1 for the Gaussian unitary ensemble (and θ_c = 1 for GOE after appropriate scaling). For a single spike θ > 1, the top eigenvalue λ_max separates from the bulk and converges almost surely to θ + 1/θ (for GUE) or to θ + 1/θ (for GOE with a factor 2 in the variance convention). Its fluctuations are Gaussian with variance of order n⁻¹, in stark contrast to the n⁻²ᐟ³ Tracy–Widom fluctuations when θ ≤ 1. At the critical value θ = 1, the top eigenvalue exhibits a crossover distribution that interpolates between Tracy–Widom and Gaussian; this distribution can be expressed in terms of a Painlevé II transcendent with a parameter. For multiple spikes, the eigenvalues separate sequentially as each θ_k crosses 1, and the joint distribution of the outliers is asymptotically independent Gaussian. The BBP transition has a precise counterpart in sample covariance matrices: for a population covariance Σ = I + Σk=1^r β_k v_k v_k^T, the sample eigenvalues exhibit a phase transition at β_k = √γ (where γ = p/n). Johnstone’s theorem (2001) shows that the largest sample eigenvalue follows the Tracy–Widom law (β = 1 for real data, β = 2 for complex) when all β_k ≤ √γ, and a Gaussian law when a spike exceeds the threshold. The detection boundary θ_c = 1 (or √γ for covariance) is sharp: no statistical test can reliably distinguish a spike below the threshold from pure noise. This result underpins modern high‑dimensional hypothesis testing, principal component analysis, and community detection in networks.

Free Probability and the R‑Transform

Free probability, introduced by Voiculescu, provides an algebraic framework for computing the asymptotic eigenvalue distribution of sums and products of large random matrices that are asymptotically free. Two sequences of random matrices Aₙ and Bₙ are asymptotically free if mixed moments factorise in the limit n → ∞. The central object is the Cauchy (Stieltjes) transform G(z) = τ((z − X)⁻¹), where τ is the normalized trace. The R‑transform R(w) is defined implicitly by G(R(w) + 1/w) = w, and it linearises free additive convolution: if X and Y are free, then RX+Y(w) = R_X(w) + R_Y(w). For the semicircle law, R(w) = w; for the Marchenko–Pastur law with parameter γ, R(w) = 1/(1 − γ w). This machinery yields the limiting spectral density of sums such as a Wigner matrix plus a deterministic diagonal matrix, or of products such as X Y where X and Y are independent Wishart matrices. The S‑transform linearises free multiplicative convolution: SXY(w) = S_X(w) S_Y(w). Free probability also gives a systematic way to compute the outlier eigenvalues in spiked models: the equation 1/θ = G_sc(λ) determines the location of a spike θ outside the support of the semicircle. The subordination property — the Cauchy transform of the sum is the composition of the individual Cauchy transforms with analytic subordination functions — provides a powerful analytic tool for proving local laws for deformed ensembles. While free probability operates at the level of global spectral distributions, recent work combines it with the Green function comparison method to obtain local laws and universality for a broad class of non‑Gaussian, non‑Wigner ensembles, including random matrices with correlated entries and certain block‑structured models.

Spectral Statistics of Non‑Hermitian Random Matrices

Non‑Hermitian random matrices, such as the Ginibre ensembles (real, complex, quaternionic) with i.i.d. Gaussian entries, exhibit eigenvalue distributions in the complex plane rather than on the real line. For the complex Ginibre ensemble (GinUE), the eigenvalues form a determinantal point process with kernel K_n(z,w) = (1/π) e-(|z|²+|w|²)/2 Σk=0n-1 (z bar w)^k/k!. After scaling by √n, the empirical spectral measure converges to the circular law: uniform density on the unit disk. Local statistics in the bulk are translation invariant and given by the same kernel in the limit, leading to a sine‑kernel type repulsion in two dimensions. At the edge, the eigenvalue density drops sharply over a scale n⁻¹ᐟ², and the limiting kernel is expressed in terms of the complementary error function. For real Ginibre (GinOE), eigenvalues are either real or come in complex conjugate pairs; the real eigenvalues have a density of order n⁻¹ᐟ² near the real axis, and their spacing statistics are described by a Pfaffian point process. The non‑Hermitian analogue of the Tracy–Widom law governs the fluctuations of the eigenvalue with largest modulus: after centering at 1 and scaling by n⁻¹ᐟ², the distribution converges to a Gumbel law for GinUE and to a different extreme‑value distribution for GinOE. Recent advances have established universality of these local statistics for non‑Hermitian matrices with i.i.d. entries satisfying moment conditions, using a Hermitisation technique (Girko’s formula) that relates the logarithmic potential of the eigenvalue distribution to the Stieltjes transform of a Hermitian block matrix. This approach transfers the Green function comparison method to the non‑Hermitian setting, proving that the circular law and the local Ginibre statistics hold for a wide class of entry distributions. Applications include the stability analysis of large random dynamical systems, the spectrum of random neural network connectivity matrices, and the study of non‑normal operators in fluid dynamics.

  • Confusing the BBP threshold for Wigner matrices (θ_c = 1) with that for sample covariance matrices (β_c = √γ).
  • Assuming the Tracy–Widom distribution applies to the top eigenvalue of a spiked model for any spike strength; it only holds in the subcritical regime.
  • Mixing up the scaling exponents: bulk rigidity n⁻¹⁺ε versus edge rigidity n⁻²ᐟ³⁺ε, and the corresponding eigenvalue fluctuation scales n⁻¹ (Gaussian) versus n⁻²ᐟ³ (Tracy–Widom).
  • Treating the R‑transform as the ordinary moment generating function; it is defined via the Cauchy transform and linearises free convolution, not classical convolution.
  • Believing the circular law holds for all non‑Hermitian matrices without moment or independence assumptions; heavy‑tailed entries can produce different limiting shapes.
  • Overlooking the distinction between real and complex Ginibre ensembles: real eigenvalues appear only in the real case and have distinct spacing statistics.
  • Using the sine kernel for non‑Hermitian bulk statistics; the correct limit is the two‑dimensional Ginibre kernel, which reduces to the sine kernel only after a suitable projection.

hand/quantum-field-theory.html:
Path Integral Formulation and Functional Methods

The path integral provides a formulation of quantum field theory that is manifestly Lorentz invariant and naturally suited to gauge theories. Instead of promoting fields to operators, one computes transition amplitudes by summing over all classical field configurations weighted by the phase factor exp(iS/ħ), where S is the classical action. For a scalar field the generating functional is Z[J] = ∫𝒟φ exp[i∫d⁴x (L + Jφ)]. Functional differentiation with respect to the source J yields correlation functions: ⟨0|T{φ(x₁)…φ(xₙ)}|0⟩ = (1/Z[0]) δⁿZ[J]/δJ(x₁)…δJ(xₙ) |J=0. Gaussian integrals give the free propagator, while interactions appear as vertices in the expansion of the exponential of the interaction part of the action. The functional determinant arising from gauge fixing leads to Faddeev–Popov ghost fields, which cancel unphysical gauge degrees of freedom in loops. The path integral also makes the derivation of Ward–Takahashi identities straightforward: invariance of the functional measure under a symmetry transformation implies relations among Green’s functions that encode the quantum version of Noether’s theorem.

Gauge Fixing and Ghosts

In a non‑Abelian Yang–Mills theory the naive functional integral overcounts gauge‑equivalent configurations. One inserts a gauge‑fixing condition Fᵃ(A)=0 via a delta functional and the associated Faddeev–Popov determinant det(δFᵃ/δαᵇ). Exponentiating this determinant introduces anticommuting scalar ghost fields cᵃ, c̄ᵃ with Lagrangian L_ghost = c̄ᵃ (∂ᵘDᵘ)ᵃᵇ cᵇ. Ghosts propagate in loops but never appear as external states, ensuring unitarity of the physical S‑matrix. The BRST symmetry, a nilpotent fermionic transformation mixing gauge fields, ghosts and antighosts, provides a powerful algebraic tool to prove renormalizability and to derive Slavnov–Taylor identities that generalize Ward identities to non‑Abelian gauge theories.

Renormalization Group and Running Couplings

The renormalization group (RG) describes how the effective parameters of a quantum field theory change with the energy scale at which the theory is probed. Starting from a bare Lagrangian defined at an ultraviolet cutoff Λ, one integrates out momentum shells to obtain a Wilsonian effective action at a lower scale μ. The couplings gᵢ(μ) then obey differential equations μ dgᵢ/dμ = βᵢ(g), where the β‑functions encode the quantum corrections. In QED the one‑loop β‑function is positive, β(e) = e³/(12π²), so the fine‑structure constant grows slowly with energy. In contrast, non‑Abelian gauge theories with sufficiently few fermion flavours have a negative β‑function, β(g) = −(11/3)C_A g³/(16π²) + …, leading to asymptotic freedom: the coupling becomes weak at high momentum transfer, a property confirmed by deep‑inelastic scattering. The RG also governs the scaling behaviour near critical points in statistical physics, where the same formalism describes universality classes.

Fixed Points and Universality

A zero of the β‑function corresponds to a scale‑invariant theory. The Gaussian fixed point (all couplings zero) is trivial; interacting fixed points, such as the Wilson–Fisher fixed point in φ⁴ theory in three dimensions, control second‑order phase transitions. Linearising the RG flow around a fixed point yields critical exponents that are independent of microscopic details, explaining why diverse systems (magnets, fluids, alloys) share the same exponents. In four‑dimensional gauge theories the only perturbatively accessible fixed point is the Gaussian one, but supersymmetric extensions or large‑N limits can exhibit conformal fixed points with exact scale invariance.

Worked Example: One‑Loop β‑Function in QCD
Compute the one‑loop β‑function for an SU(N) gauge theory with n_f Dirac fermions in the fundamental representation.
The gauge boson self‑energy receives contributions from the gluon loop, the ghost loop and the fermion loop. Using dimensional regularisation in d = 4 − ε dimensions, the divergent part of the gluon vacuum polarization is proportional to (11/3)C_A − (4/3)T_R n_f, where C_A = N and T_R = 1/2. The renormalisation constant Z_g for the coupling g satisfies Z_g = 1 − (g²/(16π²ε))[(11/3)C_A − (4/3)T_R n_f]. The β‑function follows from β(g) = −ε g + g μ d ln Z_g/dμ, giving β(g) = −g³/(16π²)[(11/3)N − (2/3)n_f]. For QCD with N = 3 and n_f = 6 the coefficient is negative, confirming asymptotic freedom.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the sign of the β‑function, recall that gauge boson loops (including ghosts) contribute with a positive sign to the coefficient of −g³, while fermion loops contribute with a negative sign. Memorise the group‑theory factors C_A = N and T_R = 1/2 for SU(N) fundamentals; they appear in every textbook derivation and in multiple‑choice options.

Anomalies and Ward Identities

Classical symmetries can fail to survive quantisation when the functional measure is not invariant under the corresponding transformation. This phenomenon is called an anomaly. The most famous example is the axial U(1) anomaly in massless QED: the classical conservation law ∂ᵘJ⁵ᵤ = 0 is violated at one loop by ∂ᵘJ⁵ᵤ = (e²/16π²) εμνρσFμνFρσ. The anomaly is exact — higher loops do not modify the coefficient — a result known as the Adler–Bardeen non‑renormalisation theorem. In the Standard Model, gauge anomalies must cancel for the theory to be consistent. The condition ∑_L Q_L³ − ∑_R Q_R³ = 0 for each gauge group factor is satisfied by the observed fermion content, providing a powerful constraint on possible extensions. Anomalies also underlie the decay π⁰ → γγ, where the axial anomaly gives a prediction for the decay width that matches experiment.

Ward–Takahashi and Slavnov–Taylor Identities

Ward identities are the quantum counterparts of Noether currents. In QED they relate the vertex function Γᵘ(p′,p) to the derivative of the electron propagator: qᵤ Γᵘ(p+q,p) = S⁻¹(p+q) − S⁻¹(p). This guarantees the photon remains massless and the electric charge is not renormalised by vertex corrections alone. In non‑Abelian theories the Slavnov–Taylor identities, derived from BRST invariance, play the same role and enforce relations among gauge‑boson, ghost and fermion Green’s functions. They are essential for proving that the renormalisation of the gauge coupling can be absorbed into a single parameter, preserving gauge invariance order by order.

Effective Field Theories and Power Counting

When a theory contains widely separated mass scales, one can integrate out the heavy fields to obtain an effective field theory (EFT) valid below the heavy threshold. The resulting Lagrangian contains an infinite tower of higher‑dimensional operators suppressed by powers of the heavy scale M: L_eff = L_ren + Σ_i (c_i/Md_i−4) O_i, where d_i is the operator dimension. Power counting organises calculations: at a given order in E/M only a finite number of operators contribute. The classic example is the Fermi theory of weak interactions, where the W boson is integrated out, yielding a four‑fermion operator of dimension six with coefficient G_F/√2. Loop corrections in the EFT generate logarithms of μ/M that are resummed by the RG, reproducing the leading logarithms of the full theory. Chiral perturbation theory applies the same logic to the low‑energy dynamics of QCD, with pions as Goldstone bosons of spontaneously broken chiral symmetry.

Matching and Running

Matching conditions are imposed at the scale μ ≈ M to ensure that the EFT reproduces the full theory’s amplitudes up to the desired order. The Wilson coefficients c_i(μ) then run according to the anomalous‑dimension matrix of the operator basis. This framework underlies precision flavour physics (e.g. the weak effective Hamiltonian for B‑meson decays) and the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT), where dimension‑six operators parameterise possible new physics at the TeV scale.

Non‑Perturbative Methods: Instantons and Lattice QCD

Perturbation theory expands around the trivial vacuum and cannot capture phenomena such as confinement, chiral symmetry breaking or the θ‑vacuum structure of QCD. Instantons are finite‑action solutions of the Euclidean Yang–Mills equations that interpolate between topologically distinct vacua. They carry integer topological charge Q = (1/32π²)∫ d⁴x εμνρσ Tr(FμνFρσ) and contribute to the path integral with weight exp(−8π²/g²). In the dilute instanton gas approximation they generate the ’t Hooft effective vertex that violates axial U(1) symmetry, explaining the η′ mass. Lattice gauge theory provides a first‑principles non‑perturbative definition: spacetime is discretised on a hypercubic grid, the gauge links become group elements, and the functional integral becomes a high‑dimensional statistical sum evaluated by Monte Carlo importance sampling. Lattice calculations have determined the hadron spectrum, the strong coupling constant α_s at the Z pole, and the QCD equation of state at finite temperature, all in agreement with experiment.

Sign Problem and Future Directions

A major limitation of lattice QCD at finite baryon chemical potential is the sign problem: the fermion determinant becomes complex, preventing probabilistic Monte Carlo sampling. Various work‑arounds (reweighting, Taylor expansion, imaginary chemical potential, complex Langevin) have limited reach. Overcoming the sign problem remains an active research frontier, as does the development of tensor‑network and quantum‑computing approaches to non‑perturbative gauge dynamics.

  • Confusing the sign of the β‑function: remember gauge boson loops give a negative contribution to β(g) in non‑Abelian theories, while fermion loops give a positive contribution.
  • Forgetting that anomalies must cancel in the full Standard Model; a single generation would be anomalous.
  • Treating higher‑dimensional operators in an EFT as equally important without power counting in E/M.
  • Assuming instanton effects are perturbative in the coupling; they are exponentially suppressed as exp(−8π²/g²).
  • Neglecting the role of BRST symmetry in proving renormalisability of gauge theories.
  • Misapplying the Ward identity to non‑Abelian vertices without including ghost contributions.
  • Understanding that lattice QCD provides a non‑perturbative definition of the theory and has quantitatively reproduced the hadron spectrum.

hand/extended-tft.html:
Higher Categorical Foundations of Extended TQFT

The cobordism hypothesis is formulated in the language of symmetric monoidal (∞,n)-categories. The source category Bordnfr has objects 0‑manifolds, 1‑morphisms 1‑dimensional cobordisms, up to n‑morphisms given by diffeomorphism classes of n‑dimensional cobordisms with corners. Composition is given by gluing along boundaries, and the symmetric monoidal structure is disjoint union. The target category C is any symmetric monoidal (∞,n)-category with duals — typical examples are the (∞,n)-category of n‑vector spaces, the (∞,n)-category of chain complexes, or the (∞,n)-category of higher categories itself.

A fully extended TQFT is a symmetric monoidal functor Z: Bordnfr → C. The cobordism hypothesis asserts that the ∞‑groupoid of such functors is equivalent to the ∞‑groupoid of fully dualizable objects of C. An object X ∈ C is fully dualizable when it admits a dual X∨, the evaluation and coevaluation maps have adjoints, and this process continues up to level n. In practice this means X must be n‑dualizable: it has a dual, the dual has a dual, and so on, with all higher adjunctions existing and satisfying the swallowtail identities. The framing condition on Bordnfr is essential because the (∞,n)-category of framed cobordisms is the free symmetric monoidal (∞,n)-category with duals on a single object. For oriented or unoriented theories one replaces Bordnfr by the homotopy quotient Bordnfr // O(n) and the classification becomes fully dualizable objects equipped with an O(n)-homotopy fixed point structure.

The proof by Lurie uses the (∞,n)-category of correspondences and the theory of (∞,n)-categories of spans. The key step is to show that Bordnfr is the free symmetric monoidal (∞,n)-category with duals on one generator. This is achieved by analyzing the (∞,n)-category of manifolds with corners and using the Pontryagin–Thom construction to identify the space of objects with the sphere spectrum. The result reduces the classification of extended TQFTs to a purely algebraic problem: find all fully dualizable objects in a given target. For C = nVectk (the (∞,n)-category of n‑vector spaces over a field k) the fully dualizable objects are precisely the separable Frobenius algebras in (n‑1)Vectk, which in low dimensions recover the familiar classifications: 1‑dimensional theories correspond to finite‑dimensional vector spaces, 2‑dimensional theories to Calabi–Yau categories, and 3‑dimensional theories to modular tensor categories.

Understanding the higher categorical machinery is crucial for examiners who ask for the precise meaning of “fully dualizable” or for the role of the framing. A common twist is to ask why the hypothesis fails for non‑framed manifolds without the O(n)‑action, or to require the student to explain how the swallowtail identities guarantee the existence of all higher adjoints.

Invertible TQFTs, Anomalies, and the Classification of Symmetry-Protected Phases

An invertible TQFT is a symmetric monoidal functor Z: BordnG → C where the target C is the (∞,n)-category of (n‑1)-truncated spectra (or more concretely, the Picard ∞‑groupoid of C). Such theories assign invertible objects to closed manifolds and are classified by the Anderson dual of the bordism spectrum M G. The Freed–Hopkins theorem identifies the group of deformation classes of invertible n‑dimensional TQFTs with symmetry G as the group of homotopy classes of maps from the Madsen–Tillmann spectrum M T G to the Anderson dual of the sphere spectrum Iℤ. In physical language, these are precisely the symmetry‑protected topological (SPT) phases.

The cobordism hypothesis for invertible theories simplifies because a fully dualizable object in a Picard ∞‑groupoid is just an invertible object; all higher duals are automatically present. The classification then reduces to computing the homotopy groups π−n(Iℤ ∧ M T G). For G = O (unoriented), G = SO (oriented), or G = Spin, these groups are known in low dimensions and match the periodic table of topological insulators and superconductors. For example, in 3 dimensions with time‑reversal symmetry (Pin+ structure) the group is ℤ2, corresponding to the topological insulator protected by time‑reversal symmetry.

Anomalies appear when a theory defined on a manifold with boundary cannot be extended to a closed manifold; the anomaly is measured by an invertible (n+1)-dimensional TQFT. The anomaly inflow mechanism states that the boundary theory is well‑defined only when coupled to a bulk invertible theory whose partition function cancels the anomaly. In the language of the cobordism hypothesis, an anomalous theory corresponds to a map BordnG → C that does not factor through the trivial theory, and the obstruction lives in the group of invertible (n+1)-dimensional theories. This perspective unifies the classification of ’t Hooft anomalies, SPT phases, and invertible TQFTs.

Examiners often test the ability to translate between physical terminology (SPT phase, anomaly, topological insulator) and the mathematical classification via bordism groups. A typical question asks to compute the group of 2‑dimensional invertible fermionic theories with spin structure, which is ℤ2 generated by the Arf invariant, or to explain why the 4‑dimensional oriented invertible theories are classified by the signature modulo 16.

Identifying the invertible TQFT for a given SPT phase
A 3‑dimensional bosonic SPT phase with ℤ2 symmetry is described by a group cohomology class in H4(Bℤ2; U(1)) ≅ ℤ2. Using the cobordism hypothesis for invertible theories, determine the corresponding invertible TQFT and its partition function on a closed oriented 3‑manifold M equipped with a principal ℤ2-bundle.
The classification of invertible 3‑dimensional oriented TQFTs with ℤ2 symmetry is given by the bordism group Ω3SO(Bℤ2) ≅ ℤ2. The non‑trivial element is represented by the mapping torus of the non‑trivial ℤ2 action on S2. The associated invertible TQFT assigns to a closed 3‑manifold M with a ℤ2-bundle the partition function Z(M) = (−1)∫M w1 ∪ w2, where w1, w2 are the first and second Stiefel–Whitney classes of the ℤ2-bundle. This is the Dijkgraaf–Witten theory with gauge group ℤ2 and the non‑trivial 3‑cocycle. The partition function evaluates to −1 on the generator of Ω3SO(Bℤ2) and +1 on the trivial bundle, matching the group cohomology classification.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question asks for the classification of invertible TQFTs or SPT phases, first identify the symmetry type (O, SO, Spin, Pin±, or a finite group G). Then recall the relevant bordism group ΩnG or the cohomology group Hn+1(BG; U(1)) for finite groups. Write down the known low‑dimensional results: Ω1SO=0, Ω2SO=0, Ω3SO=0, Ω4SO=ℤ (signature). For fermionic symmetries use the spin bordism groups: Ω2Spin=ℤ2 (Arf), Ω3Spin=0, Ω4Spin=ℤ (signature/16). Memorise these four rows; they cover the majority of exam questions on anomalies and SPT phases.

Factorization Homology and the Construction of Extended TQFTs

Factorization homology, developed by Ayala and Francis, provides a systematic method to produce extended TQFTs from algebraic data encoded in En-algebras. Given an En-algebra A in a symmetric monoidal (∞,1)-category C (for instance, chain complexes), the factorization homology ∫M A assigns to each n‑manifold M an object of C. The assignment M ↦ ∫M A extends to a symmetric monoidal functor Bordnfr → C, i.e. a fully extended framed TQFT. The cobordism hypothesis guarantees that every fully extended framed TQFT arises in this way from a fully dualizable object, and the En-algebra A is precisely the value of the TQFT on the point, equipped with its natural En-structure coming from the little n‑disks operad action on the point.

Concretely, for n = 2 an E2-algebra is a braided monoidal category; factorization homology over a surface Σ computes the Hochschild homology of the category, which recovers the Reshetikhin–Turaev TQFT when the category is modular. For n = 3 an E3-algebra is a symmetric monoidal 2‑category; the factorization homology of a 3‑manifold yields the Turaev–Viro state sum when the input is a spherical fusion category viewed as an E3-algebra in 2Vect. The Ran space construction underlies the definition: one integrates the algebra over the configuration space of points in M, using the En-structure to multiply contributions when points collide. This locality property is exactly the physical requirement that the theory be defined by a local Lagrangian.

The factorization homology perspective clarifies the relationship between different constructions. The Drinfeld center Z(C) of a fusion category C carries a natural E2-structure, and the factorization homology of Z(C) over a 3‑manifold reproduces the Turaev–Viro invariant of C. Meanwhile, the same Drinfeld center is a modular tensor category, and its factorization homology as an E2-algebra gives the Reshetikhin–Turaev invariant. Thus factorization homology unifies the two state‑sum models and explains their equivalence as a consequence of the cobordism hypothesis applied to the fully dualizable object Z(C) in 3Vect.

Examiners may ask to describe the En-structure on the value of a TQFT at a point, or to explain why factorization homology of an En-algebra automatically satisfies the gluing axiom. A typical trap is to confuse the little n‑disks operad (which governs En-algebras) with the framed little n‑disks operad (which governs framed En-algebras); the latter is required for the framed cobordism hypothesis.

The Drinfeld Center and the Equivalence of Turaev-Viro and Reshetikhin-Turaev Theories

The Drinfeld center Z(C) of a spherical fusion category C is a modular tensor category. Its simple objects are pairs (X, γ) where X ∈ C and γ is a half‑braiding, i.e. a natural isomorphism X ⊗ Y → Y ⊗ X satisfying the hexagon axioms. The braiding in Z(C) is induced by the half‑braiding, and the S‑matrix is non‑degenerate, making Z(C) modular. The Turaev–Viro TQFT built from C assigns to a closed 3‑manifold M the state sum ZTV(M) = Σlabelings Πtetrahedra {6j‑symbol}C. The Reshetikhin–Turaev TQFT built from Z(C) assigns ZRT(M) computed via surgery presentations and the modular data of Z(C). The theorem of Barrett–Westbury and later of Müger states that ZTV(M) = ZRT(M) for all closed oriented 3‑manifolds M.

The proof uses the fact that the Turaev–Viro state sum can be interpreted as the partition function of a 3‑dimensional TQFT whose value on the point is C, viewed as an object in the 3‑category of fusion categories. The Drinfeld center Z(C) is the image of C under the fully dualizable object construction in the 3‑category of tensor categories; it is the “higher center” that makes C fully dualizable. The cobordism hypothesis then implies that the extended TQFT determined by C factors through the extended TQFT determined by Z(C). At the level of 3‑manifold invariants this factorization yields the equality of the two state sums.

An important corollary is that the Turaev–Viro invariant is always a perfect square of the Reshetikhin–Turaev invariant when the modular category is the Drinfeld center of a spherical fusion category: ZTV(M) = |ZRT(M)|2. This follows because the Turaev–Viro theory is the “doubled” theory obtained by stacking the Reshetikhin–Turaev theory with its orientation reverse. In the language of extended TQFTs, the Turaev–Viro theory corresponds to the fully dualizable object C in 3Vect, while the Reshetikhin–Turaev theory corresponds to the fully dualizable object Z(C) in 3Vect; the two are Morita equivalent, and the Morita equivalence is implemented by the bimodule category C itself.

Exam questions often ask to compute the quantum dimension of the Drinfeld center in terms of the quantum dimensions of C: dim Z(C) = (dim C)2. Another common task is to verify that the 6j‑symbols of C satisfy the pentagon and hexagon equations that guarantee the modularity of Z(C). Students should be comfortable translating between the graphical calculus of fusion categories and the algebraic data of the modular S‑ and T‑matrices.

Extended TQFTs in Low Dimensions: Explicit Classifications and Computational Tools

In dimension 1, a fully extended framed TQFT Z: Bord1fr → C is determined by a fully dualizable object in C. For C = Vectk the fully dualizable objects are precisely the finite‑dimensional vector spaces; the theory assigns to a point the vector space V, to an interval the identity map, and to a circle the trace of the identity, i.e. dim V. The classification is therefore equivalent to the choice of a finite‑dimensional vector space.

In dimension 2, the target is often taken to be the 2‑category of linear categories, bimodules, and intertwiners. Fully dualizable objects are Calabi–Yau categories: finite semisimple categories equipped with a non‑degenerate trace. The corresponding 2‑dimensional TQFT is the A‑model or B‑model topological string, and the partition function on a genus‑g surface is the dimension of the space of conformal blocks. The classification of 2‑dimensional oriented TQFTs reduces to commutative Frobenius algebras, a classic result of Dijkgraaf and Moore–Segal.

In dimension 3, the fully dualizable objects in 3Vect are modular tensor categories. The Reshetikhin–Turaev construction produces the extended TQFT from a modular tensor category, while the Turaev–Viro construction produces the extended TQFT from a spherical fusion category (which is not fully dualizable in 3Vect but becomes so after passing to its Drinfeld center). The Crane–Yetter invariant in dimension 4 uses a braided fusion category, which is a fully dualizable object in 4Vect. The pattern continues: in dimension n the algebraic input is an En-algebra in (n‑1)Vect that is fully dualizable.

Computational tools include the use of the 6j‑symbols for state sums, the modular S‑ and T‑matrices for surgery calculations, and the factorization homology software packages that automate the evaluation of ∫M A for triangulated manifolds. For topological quantum computing, the braiding matrices derived from the modular data provide explicit gate sets; the Fibonacci anyon model corresponds to the modular category SU(2)3 (or the Yang–Lee category), and its braiding matrices are dense in the unitary group on the fusion space.

Examiners frequently test the ability to match a given algebraic structure (Frobenius algebra, modular tensor category, braided fusion category) to the dimension of the TQFT it classifies, and to explain why a spherical fusion category alone does not give a fully extended 3‑dimensional TQFT without passing to its Drinfeld center. A typical twist is to ask for the obstruction to extending a 2‑dimensional TQFT to a 3‑dimensional one, which is the non‑vanishing of the anomaly measured by the modular central charge.

  • Confusing the framed cobordism hypothesis with the oriented version; the framed hypothesis classifies theories with a trivialization of the tangent bundle, while the oriented version requires an SO(n)-homotopy fixed point.
  • Assuming every fusion category yields a fully extended 3‑dimensional TQFT; only the Drinfeld center (a modular tensor category) is fully dualizable in 3Vect.
  • Misidentifying the En-structure: an E2-algebra is braided monoidal, an E3-algebra is symmetric monoidal; the little n‑disks operad governs the former, the framed little n‑disks operad the latter.
  • Overlooking the role of the anomaly: an anomalous theory does not define a functor on the full cobordism category but only on a category with boundary, and the anomaly is an invertible (n+1)-dimensional theory.
  • Treating the Turaev–Viro and Reshetikhin–Turaev invariants as independent; they are equal when the modular category is the Drinfeld center of the spherical fusion category, and the Turaev–Viro invariant is the squared modulus of the Reshetikhin–Turaev invariant.
  • Forgetting that the quantum dimension of the Drinfeld center is the square of the quantum dimension of the original fusion category: dim Z(C) = (dim C)2.
  • Confusing the classification of invertible TQFTs (bordism groups) with the classification of fully extended TQFTs (fully dualizable objects); the former are a special case where the target is a Picard ∞‑groupoid.

Mastering these distinctions and computational techniques ensures a solid grasp of the modern mathematical framework underlying topological quantum field theory and its applications to condensed matter and quantum computation.

hand/lie-theory.html:
Parabolic Subgroups, Flag Varieties, and the Bruhat Decomposition

A parabolic subgroup of a complex semisimple Lie group G is a closed subgroup containing a Borel subgroup B. Equivalently, its Lie algebra 𝔭 is a subalgebra of 𝔤 containing a Borel subalgebra 𝔟. Parabolic subalgebras are in bijection with subsets of the simple roots Π: for a subset Θ ⊆ Π, the standard parabolic 𝔭_Θ is generated by 𝔟 together with the negative root spaces 𝔤−α for α ∈ Θ. The corresponding parabolic subgroup P_Θ has Levi decomposition P_Θ = L_Θ ⋉ U_Θ, where L_Θ is the reductive Levi factor (generated by the Cartan subalgebra and root spaces for roots in the span of Θ) and U_Θ is the unipotent radical (generated by positive root spaces not in the span of Θ). The quotient G/P_Θ is a projective algebraic variety called a generalized flag variety; when Θ = ∅ it is the full flag variety G/B, and when Θ = Π it is a point.

The Bruhat decomposition gives a cellular decomposition of G/P_Θ indexed by the cosets W/W_Θ, where W is the Weyl group and W_Θ the subgroup generated by simple reflections in Θ. For each coset wW_Θ there is a Bruhat cell C_w = B w P_Θ / P_Θ isomorphic to an affine space of dimension ℓ(w), the length of the minimal coset representative. The closure relations among cells are governed by the Bruhat order on W/W_Θ. This decomposition yields a stratification of the flag variety by Schubert varieties X_w = C_w, whose cohomology classes [X_w] form a ℤ-basis of H^*(G/P_Θ, ℤ). The multiplication in cohomology corresponds to the Schubert calculus, which can be expressed via the Littlewood–Richardson rule for Grassmannians and more generally via the structure constants of the nil-Hecke ring.

Line bundles on G/P_Θ are classified by characters of P_Θ, which correspond to weights λ ∈ 𝔥^* that are dominant with respect to Θ. The Borel–Weil–Bott theorem computes the sheaf cohomology of these line bundles: for a dominant weight λ, H0(G/P_Θ, ℒ_λ) is the irreducible representation V(λ) of highest weight λ, while higher cohomology vanishes. If λ is not dominant, there is a unique w ∈ W such that w(λ+ρ)−ρ is dominant, and Hℓ(w)(G/P_Θ, ℒ_λ) ≅ V(w(λ+ρ)−ρ) with all other groups zero. This geometric realization underpins the proof of the Weyl character formula via the Atiyah–Bott fixed point theorem on G/B.

Parabolic induction and its derived functors (Zuckerman functors) provide a bridge between representations of G and those of its Levi subgroups. The Bernstein–Gelfand–Gelfand category 𝒪 can be realized as the category of (𝔤, K)-modules with a compatible action of the center of U(𝔤), and the translation functors across walls of the Weyl chambers correspond to tensoring with finite-dimensional representations and projecting onto blocks. The Kazhdan–Lusztig conjecture (proved by Beilinson–Bernstein and Brylinski–Kashiwara) expresses the characters of simple highest weight modules in terms of intersection cohomology of Schubert varieties, linking representation theory to the geometry of the flag variety.

Chevalley–Eilenberg Cohomology and Lie Algebra Extensions

The Chevalley–Eilenberg complex computes the Lie algebra cohomology H^*(𝔤, M) for a 𝔤-module M. For a finite-dimensional Lie algebra 𝔤 over a field of characteristic zero, the cochain groups are C^n(𝔤, M) = Hom(∧^n 𝔤, M) with differential d defined by (dφ)(x1,…,xn+1) = Σ_i (−1)i+1 x_i·φ(x1,…,x̂_i,…,xn+1) + Σi<j</sub> (−1)i+j φ([x_i,x_j], x1,…,x̂_i,…,x̂_j,…,xn+1). The resulting cohomology groups classify infinitesimal deformations and extensions: H1(𝔤, M) ≅ Der(𝔤, M)/InnDer(𝔤, M) measures outer derivations, while H2(𝔤, M) classifies equivalence classes of extensions 0 → M → 𝔢 → 𝔤 → 0 of Lie algebras with abelian kernel M. The Whitehead lemmas state that for a semisimple Lie algebra 𝔤 and any finite-dimensional module M, H1(𝔤, M) = H2(𝔤, M) = 0; consequently every derivation is inner and every extension splits, reflecting the rigidity of semisimple algebras.

For a solvable or nilpotent Lie algebra, cohomology can be nontrivial. The cohomology of the Heisenberg algebra 𝔥_n (dimension 2n+1) with trivial coefficients is isomorphic to the exterior algebra on 2n generators in degree 1 and one generator in degree 2, reflecting its central extension structure. The Hochschild–Serre spectral sequence relates the cohomology of an extension 𝔢 to that of the ideal 𝔞 and the quotient 𝔤/𝔞: E2p,q = H^p(𝔤/𝔞, H^q(𝔞, M)) ⇒ Hp+q(𝔢, M). This tool is essential for computing cohomology of parabolic subalgebras and for the proof of the Kostant theorem, which identifies H^*(𝔫, ℂ) for the nilradical 𝔫 of a Borel subalgebra as the cohomology of the flag variety G/B.

Kostant's theorem states that as a representation of the Cartan subalgebra 𝔥, H^q(𝔫, ℂ) ≅ ⊕w∈W, ℓ(w)=q ℂw(ρ)−ρ, where the sum runs over Weyl group elements of length q. This gives a Lie algebra cohomology interpretation of the Bruhat decomposition and provides a purely algebraic proof of the Weyl character formula via the Euler characteristic of the complex. The theorem extends to parabolic nilradicals: for a standard parabolic 𝔭 = 𝔩 ⊕ 𝔲, the cohomology H^*(𝔲, ℂ) decomposes into a direct sum of irreducible 𝔩-modules indexed by the quotient W/W_Θ, with highest weights given by w(ρ)−ρ for minimal coset representatives w. This result underlies the Borel–Weil–Bott theorem and the construction of Zuckerman's derived functor modules A_𝔮(λ).

Lie algebra cohomology also appears in the study of invariant differential operators on symmetric spaces. The relative Lie algebra cohomology H^*(𝔤, K; V) for a (𝔤, K)-module V computes the cohomology of the associated vector bundle on the symmetric space G/K. Matsushima's formula expresses the de Rham cohomology of a locally symmetric space ΓG/K in terms of (𝔤, K)-cohomology of automorphic representations, linking representation theory to the topology of arithmetic quotients.

Worked Example: Computing the Bruhat Cell Dimension in SL(3, ℂ)
Let G = SL(3, ℂ) with Borel subgroup B of upper triangular matrices. The Weyl group W ≅ S3 has six elements. For the simple reflection s1 corresponding to the transposition (1 2), determine the dimension of the Bruhat cell Cs1 = B s1 B / B in the full flag variety G/B.
The length ℓ(s1) equals the number of positive roots sent to negative roots by s1. The positive roots of SL(3) are α1 = ε1−ε2, α2 = ε2−ε3, α1+α2 = ε1−ε3. The reflection s1 swaps ε1 and ε2, so s1(α1) = −α1 (negative), s1(α2) = α1+α2 (positive), s1(α1+α2) = α2 (positive). Exactly one positive root becomes negative, hence ℓ(s1) = 1. The Bruhat cell Cs1 is isomorphic to an affine space of dimension 1. Therefore dim Cs1 = 1.
Exam Strategy
When asked for the dimension of a Bruhat cell, compute the length of the minimal coset representative in the Weyl group. For classical groups, length equals the number of inversions in the corresponding permutation or signed permutation. Memorize the length formula for type A (inversions) and type B/C/D (inversions plus sign changes) to answer quickly.

Quantum Groups and Drinfeld–Jimbo Deformations

Quantum groups are noncommutative, noncocommutative Hopf algebras that deform the universal enveloping algebra U(𝔤) of a semisimple Lie algebra 𝔤. The Drinfeld–Jimbo quantum group U_q(𝔤) is generated by elements E_i, F_i, K_i±1 (i = 1,…,rank) subject to relations: K_i K_i-1 = 1, K_i E_j K_i-1 = qaij E_j, K_i F_j K_i-1 = q−aij F_j, [E_i, F_j] = δij (K_i − K_i-1)/(q_i − q_i-1), and the quantum Serre relations Σk=01−aij (−1)^k [1−aij choose k]q_i E_i^k E_j E_i1−aij−k = 0 (and similarly for F_i). Here aij are the Cartan matrix entries, q_i = qd_i with d_i the symmetrizing integers, and the q-binomial coefficients are defined via the quantum integer [n]_q = (q^n − q−n)/(q − q−1). The Hopf algebra structure is given by Δ(E_i) = E_i ⊗ 1 + K_i ⊗ E_i, Δ(F_i) = F_i ⊗ K_i-1 + 1 ⊗ F_i, Δ(K_i) = K_i ⊗ K_i, with counit ε(E_i)=ε(F_i)=0, ε(K_i)=1 and antipode S(E_i)=−K_i-1E_i, S(F_i)=−F_i K_i, S(K_i)=K_i-1. As q → 1, U_q(𝔤) recovers U(𝔤).

Finite-dimensional representation theory of U_q(𝔤) for generic q (not a root of unity) mirrors the classical highest weight theory: irreducible modules V_q(λ) are indexed by dominant integral weights λ, have the same dimension as their classical counterparts, and their characters are given by the same Weyl character formula with q-exponentials. The tensor product of two such modules decomposes with the same Clebsch–Gordan multiplicities, but the braiding is nontrivial: the universal R-matrix ℛ ∈ U_q(𝔤) ⊗ U_q(𝔤) satisfies ℛ Δ(x) = Δop(x) ℛ and provides a braided monoidal structure on the category of representations. This braiding yields solutions of the quantum Yang–Baxter equation and underlies the construction of knot invariants (Jones polynomial, HOMFLY-PT) via the Reshetikhin–Turaev functor.

At roots of unity, the representation theory changes dramatically. If q is a primitive ℓ-th root of unity with ℓ odd and coprime to the determinant of the Cartan matrix, the center of U_q(𝔤) becomes large, and the category of finite-dimensional modules is no longer semisimple. The small quantum group u_q(𝔤) (the quotient by the ideal generated by E_i^ℓ, F_i^ℓ, K_i^ℓ−1) is a finite-dimensional Hopf algebra of dimension ℓdim 𝔤. Its representation theory is linked to the geometry of the affine flag variety and to modular tensor categories arising in conformal field theory. The Lusztig quantum Frobenius map relates u_q(𝔤) to the distribution algebra of the algebraic group G in characteristic ℓ, providing a bridge between quantum groups at roots of unity and modular representation theory.

Drinfeld's quantum double construction D(H) for a finite-dimensional Hopf algebra H produces a quasitriangular Hopf algebra. For H = U(𝔟) (the Borel subalgebra), D(U(𝔟)) is isomorphic to U_q(𝔤) after a suitable completion. This perspective explains the origin of the R-matrix and the factorization of the universal R-matrix as ℛ = ℛ0 ℛ_+, where ℛ0 = qΣ (B-1)ij H_i ⊗ H_j involves the Cartan part and ℛ_+ is an ordered product of quantum exponentials in the positive root vectors. The factorization is essential for the explicit computation of matrix elements and for the theory of quantum symmetric pairs.

Geometric Representation Theory: Beilinson–Bernstein Localization and D-modules

The Beilinson–Bernstein localization theorem establishes an equivalence between the category of (𝔤, K)-modules with a fixed central character χ_λ (where λ ∈ 𝔥^* is dominant regular) and the category of K-equivariant D-modules on the flag variety G/B twisted by the line bundle ℒ_λ. Here DG/B denotes the sheaf of algebraic differential operators, and the twist is DG/Bλ = ℒ_λ ⊗ DG/B ⊗ ℒ−λ. The global sections functor Γ(G/B, −) and the localization functor Δ_λ = DG/Bλ ⊗U(𝔤) − give the equivalence. This geometric realization transforms questions about representations into questions about D-modules, allowing the use of sheaf-theoretic methods such as the Riemann–Hilbert correspondence, perverse sheaves, and the decomposition theorem.

The theorem implies the Kazhdan–Lusztig conjecture: the character of a simple highest weight module L(λ) is given by the alternating sum of characters of Verma modules with coefficients given by Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials Py,w(1). Geometrically, these polynomials compute the stalk cohomology of intersection cohomology complexes IC(X_w) on Schubert varieties X_w ⊂ G/B. The proof uses the fact that the localization of a Verma module M(w·λ) is the D-module corresponding to the constant sheaf on the Schubert cell C_w, and the simple module L(w·λ) corresponds to the intersection cohomology complex IC(X_w). The decomposition theorem for the proper map from the Bott–Samelson resolution to X_w yields the Kazhdan–Lusztig multiplicity formula.

D-modules on G/B also encode the action of the center Z(𝔤) via the Harish-Chandra isomorphism Z(𝔤) ≅ S(𝔥)^W. The central character χ_λ acts on a D-module by the scalar λ+ρ under the identification of the cotangent bundle T^*(G/B) with the Springer resolution of the nilpotent cone 𝒩 ⊂ 𝔤^*. The characteristic variety of a (𝔤, K)-module is a K-invariant Lagrangian subvariety of 𝒩, and the associated variety of a primitive ideal is the closure of a nilpotent orbit. This links the classification of primitive ideals (Duflo's theorem) to the geometry of nilpotent orbits and the Springer correspondence.

The theory extends to real groups via the localization of (𝔤, K)-modules on the real flag variety G_ℝ/K_ℝ, leading to the construction of standard and irreducible Harish-Chandra modules. The Vogan–Zuckerman derived functor modules A_𝔮(λ) are obtained by applying Zuckerman functors to cohomologically induced modules, and their geometric counterparts are the equivariant D-modules on the partial flag variety G/P with support on K-orbits. The orbit method of Kirillov and the geometric quantization of coadjoint orbits provide a unifying picture: irreducible unitary representations correspond to quantized coadjoint orbits, and the Beilinson–Bernstein equivalence is the algebraic incarnation of this quantization for complex groups.

Nilpotent Orbits, the Jacobson–Morozov Theorem, and the Bala–Carter Classification

Nilpotent orbits in a complex semisimple Lie algebra 𝔤 are the adjoint orbits of nilpotent elements. The Jacobson–Morozov theorem states that any nilpotent element e ∈ 𝔤 can be embedded in an 𝔰𝔩2-triple {e, h, f} with [h, e] = 2e, [h, f] = −2f, [e, f] = h. The semisimple element h defines a grading 𝔤 = ⊕j∈ℤ 𝔤(j) where 𝔤(j) = {x ∈ 𝔤 | [h, x] = j x}. The centralizer 𝔷_𝔤(e) is contained in ⊕j≥0 𝔤(j), and its dimension determines the orbit dimension: dim O_e = dim 𝔤 − dim 𝔷_𝔤(e). The weighted Dynkin diagram of e assigns to each simple root α_i the integer α_i(h) ∈ {0, 1, 2}, providing a combinatorial invariant that classifies nilpotent orbits up to finitely many ambiguities.

The Bala–Carter classification gives a bijection between nilpotent orbits in 𝔤 and conjugacy classes of pairs (𝔩, 𝔭) where 𝔩 is a Levi subalgebra of a parabolic subalgebra 𝔭 and the orbit is the induced orbit Ind_𝔭^𝔤(0) (the Richardson orbit of 𝔭). Equivalently, orbits correspond to distinguished nilpotent orbits in Levi subalgebras, where an orbit is distinguished if it does not meet any proper Levi subalgebra. The classification is expressed in terms of weighted Dynkin diagrams with labels 0, 1, 2 satisfying certain admissibility conditions. For classical types, the orbits are parametrized by partitions (for types A, C) or by partitions with parity constraints (for types B, D). The closure ordering of nilpotent orbits corresponds to the dominance order on partitions.

The Springer correspondence relates the irreducible representations of the Weyl group W to pairs (O, ℒ) where O is a nilpotent orbit and ℒ is an irreducible G-equivariant local system on O. For simply-laced types, all local systems are trivial, and the correspondence gives a bijection between Irr(W) and nilpotent orbits. The top cohomology of the Springer fiber ℬ_e = {Borel subalgebras containing e} carries a W-action isomorphic to the representation corresponding to (O_e, trivial). The generalized Springer correspondence extends this to non-simply-laced types and to nontrivial local systems, linking the representation theory of W to the geometry of the nilpotent cone.

Nilpotent orbits also appear in the classification of primitive ideals via the Joseph–Goldie theory. The associated variety of a primitive ideal J is the closure of a nilpotent orbit O, and the Goldie rank polynomial rk_J(λ) gives the multiplicity of the simple module L(λ) in the associated graded module. The Lusztig–Spaltenstein induction and restriction functors on perverse sheaves on the nilpotent cone categorify the induction and restriction of Weyl group representations, providing a geometric framework for the Macdonald conjectures on affine Hecke algebras.

  • Confusing the Bruhat order on the full Weyl group with the induced order on cosets W/W_Θ when computing cell dimensions.
  • Assuming the Chevalley–Eilenberg differential vanishes on all cochains for semisimple algebras; it vanishes only on cohomology classes.
  • Treating the quantum parameter q as a formal variable without specifying whether it is generic or a root of unity, which changes the representation category drastically.
  • Overlooking the twist by the line bundle ℒ_λ in the Beilinson–Bernstein equivalence; the untwisted D-modules correspond to the trivial central character only.
  • Misidentifying the weighted Dynkin diagram labels as the coefficients of the highest root; they are the eigenvalues of the 𝔰𝔩2 semisimple element h on the simple root spaces.
  • Assuming every nilpotent orbit admits a nontrivial local system; in simply-laced types all local systems are trivial.
  • Forgetting that the Springer correspondence for non-simply-laced types requires the generalized version with nontrivial local systems.

These advanced topics complete the structural picture of Lie theory needed for research-level examinations.

hand/stochastic-proc.html:
Stochastic Filtering and the Kalman–Bucy Filter

Stochastic filtering addresses the problem of estimating the state of a partially observed dynamical system driven by noise. The classic setting: a signal process Xt satisfies a stochastic differential equation dXt = a(Xt,t)dt + b(Xt,t)dWt, while observations Yt follow dYt = h(Xt,t)dt + dVt with independent Brownian motions W, V. The goal is to compute the conditional distribution πt(·) = P(Xt ∈ · | ℱtY) where ℱtY is the σ‑algebra generated by observations up to time t. The Kushner–Stratonovich equation gives the evolution of the unnormalized conditional density; it is a nonlinear stochastic PDE. In the linear‑Gaussian case — a(x,t) = Atx, b = Bt, h(x,t) = Htx — the conditional distribution remains Gaussian, fully described by its mean m̂t and covariance Pt. The Kalman–Bucy filter provides ordinary differential equations for these moments: dm̂t = Atm̂tdt + Kt(dYt − Htm̂tdt) with gain Kt = PtHt⊤Rt−1, and dPt = (AtPt + PtAt⊤ + BtBt⊤ − PtHt⊤Rt−1HtPt)dt. This Riccati equation for Pt is deterministic; its steady‑state solution yields the algebraic Riccati equation used in infinite‑horizon filtering. The filter is optimal in the minimum mean‑square sense and forms the basis for modern navigation, tracking, and data assimilation systems.

Stochastic Optimal Control and the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman Equation

Stochastic optimal control seeks a policy u(·) minimizing an expected cost J(u) = E[∫0T f(Xt,ut,t)dt + g(XT)] subject to the controlled diffusion dXt = b(Xt,ut,t)dt + σ(Xt,ut,t)dWt. The value function V(x,t) = infu Ex,t[∫tT f + g] satisfies the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman (HJB) equation: −∂tV = infu{ f + b·∇V + ½ Tr(σσ⊤∇²V) } with terminal condition V(x,T) = g(x). The infimum is attained at a feedback control u*(x,t) = argminu{…}. Verification theorems guarantee that a sufficiently smooth solution of the HJB yields an optimal control. In the linear‑quadratic (LQ) case — b = Ax + Bu, σ constant, f = x⊤Qx + u⊤Ru, g = x⊤Sx — the value function is quadratic V = x⊤P(t)x and the Riccati equation for P(t) emerges. The optimal feedback is u* = −R−1B⊤P(t)x. For infinite horizon, the algebraic Riccati equation gives a constant gain. The HJB framework extends to risk‑sensitive control (exponential cost) and to problems with state constraints via viscosity solutions.

Worked Example: Linear‑Quadratic Regulator
Consider the scalar system dX = u dt + dW, cost J = E[∫0∞ (X² + u²)dt]. Find the optimal stationary feedback and the minimal cost.
The HJB for infinite horizon: 0 = infu{ x² + u² + u V' + ½ V'' }. The minimizer is u* = −½ V'. Substituting gives 0 = x² + ¼ V'² − ½ V'² + ½ V'' = x² − ¼ V'² + ½ V''. Try quadratic V = P x². Then V' = 2P x, V'' = 2P. Equation: x² − P²x² + P = 0 for all x. Hence P² = 1 and P = 1 (positive root). Optimal feedback u* = −x. Minimal cost V(x) = x².
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a stochastic control problem appears, first identify whether it is linear‑quadratic; if so, write the Riccati equation immediately — it yields the feedback law without solving the full HJB. For nonlinear problems, look for a verification theorem: propose a candidate value function, check smoothness, and verify the HJB inequality. Remember that the optimal control is often expressed as a function of the gradient of the value function.

Large Deviations Theory and Freidlin–Wentzell Estimates

Large deviations theory quantifies the exponential decay of probabilities of rare events for families of random processes. For a family {Xε}ε>0 on a Polish space, a rate function I : E → [0,∞] is a good rate function if its level sets are compact. The family satisfies a large deviation principle (LDP) with speed ε⁻² if for all measurable A, −infx∈A° I(x) ≤ liminfε→0 ε² log P(Xε ∈ A) ≤ limsupε→0 ε² log P(Xε ∈ A) ≤ −infx∈Ā I(x). For small‑noise diffusions dXεt = b(Xεt)dt + √ε σ(Xεt)dWt, the Freidlin–Wentzell theorem gives the rate function I0,T(φ) = ½ ∫0T |σ(φ(s))⁻¹(φ̇(s) − b(φ(s)))|² ds for absolutely continuous paths φ with φ(0)=x, and ∞ otherwise. The quasipotential V(x,y) = infT>0 infφ: φ(0)=x, φ(T)=y I0,T(φ) governs exit times from domains: for a bounded domain D with smooth boundary, the expected exit time from D starting at x satisfies limε→0 ε² log Ex[τD] = infy∈∂D V(x,y). This underpins metastability analysis in chemical kinetics, climate models, and neural networks. The contraction principle transfers LDPs through continuous maps, and Varadhan's lemma evaluates asymptotics of integrals of exponentials.

Stochastic Partial Differential Equations and the Stochastic Heat Equation

Stochastic partial differential equations (SPDEs) describe random fields evolving in space and time. The prototypical example is the stochastic heat equation on a domain D ⊂ ℝd: ∂tu = Δu + ξ, where ξ is space‑time white noise (the formal derivative of a cylindrical Wiener process on L²(D)). For d = 1, the solution is a continuous random field; for d ≥ 2, space‑time white noise is too irregular and renormalisation (e.g., Wick product) is required. The mild formulation uses the heat semigroup S(t) = etΔ: u(t) = S(t)u0 + ∫0t S(t−s)dW(s). Existence and uniqueness hold in weighted Sobolev spaces under Lipschitz nonlinearities. The invariant measure for the stochastic heat equation with additive noise is a Gaussian free field with covariance (−Δ)−1. For multiplicative noise ∂tu = Δu + u ξ, the solution exhibits intermittency: moments grow exponentially in time, and the Lyapunov exponents are given by the Feynman–Kac formula. The KPZ equation ∂th = ½ Δh + ½ |∇h|² + ξ arises as a universal scaling limit of growth models; its solution theory uses regularity structures or paracontrolled distributions. SPDEs also appear in filtering (the Kushner–Stratonovich equation) and in quantum field theory (stochastic quantisation).

Term Structure Models and Credit Risk in Mathematical Finance

Interest rate models describe the evolution of the entire yield curve. The Heath–Jarrow–Morton (HJM) framework models forward rates f(t,T) for all maturities T ≥ t via df(t,T) = α(t,T)dt + σ(t,T)·dWt. No‑arbitrage forces the drift α(t,T) = σ(t,T)·∫tT σ(t,s)ds. Short‑rate models (Vasicek, Cox–Ingersoll–Ross) are special cases where the forward curve is determined by a finite‑dimensional Markov process. The CIR model dr = κ(θ−r)dt + σ√r dW yields affine bond prices P(t,T) = eA(τ)−B(τ)r with Riccati ODEs for A,B. For credit risk, reduced‑form models specify a default intensity λt; the survival probability is E[e−∫tT λs ds]. Structural models (Merton) link default to a firm’s asset value crossing a barrier. The CreditMetrics and CreditRisk+ frameworks use copulas to model joint default correlations. Counterparty credit risk introduces credit valuation adjustment (CVA): the risk‑neutral expectation of discounted loss due to counterparty default, computed via Monte Carlo simulation of exposure profiles and intensity models. These tools are essential for pricing interest rate derivatives, managing bond portfolios, and regulatory capital calculation.

  • Confusing the Kalman–Bucy filter (continuous‑time) with the discrete‑time Kalman filter; the Riccati equation is differential, not difference.
  • Assuming the HJB equation always has a classical smooth solution; viscosity solutions are often required for verification.
  • Misapplying the Freidlin–Wentzell rate function to diffusions with degenerate noise (σ not invertible) without projecting onto the controllable subspace.
  • Treating space‑time white noise as a function rather than a distribution; in dimensions ≥2 the stochastic heat equation needs renormalisation.
  • Using the Vasicek model for long‑dated bonds without checking the positivity of rates; the CIR model preserves non‑negativity.
  • Neglecting the drift restriction in HJM; any arbitrary volatility specification must satisfy the HJM drift condition to avoid arbitrage.
  • Overlooking the difference between reduced‑form intensity models and structural models when calibrating credit spreads.

These advanced topics complete the stochastic processes toolkit for rigorous modelling of randomness in time and space.

Non‑Ideal Solution Models: Margules, van Laar and Wilson Equations

Real solutions deviate from Raoult’s law because the intermolecular forces between unlike molecules differ from those in the pure components. The simplest quantitative description uses activity coefficients (γ₁, γ₂) defined by pᵢ = xᵢ γᵢ p°ᵢ. For binary mixtures the excess Gibbs energy Gᴱ = RT (x₁ ln γ₁ + x₂ ln γ₂) is modelled by empirical equations. The two‑parameter Margules model writes Gᴱ/RT = x₁ x₂ (A₂₁ x₁ + A₁₂ x₂) giving ln γ₁ = x₂² [A₁₂ + 2 (A₂₁ – A₁₂) x₁] and ln γ₂ = x₁² [A₂₁ + 2 (A₁₂ – A₂₁) x₂]. The van Laar equation, derived from the same excess‑energy concept but assuming a different local‑composition hypothesis, yields ln γ₁ = A₁₂ / (1 + (A₁₂ x₁)/(A₂₁ x₂))² and an analogous expression for γ₂. Both models reduce to Raoult’s law when A₁₂ = A₂₁ = 0. The Wilson equation introduces a non‑randomness parameter Λᵢⱼ = (Vⱼ/Vᵢ) exp(–Δλᵢⱼ/RT) and gives ln γ₁ = –ln(x₁ + Λ₁₂ x₂) + x₂ [Λ₁₂/(x₁ + Λ₁₂ x₂) – Λ₂₁/(x₂ + Λ₂₁ x₁)]. Wilson’s form cannot predict liquid‑liquid equilibrium but works well for vapour‑liquid equilibrium of highly non‑ideal systems such as ethanol–water. Parameters Aᵢⱼ or Λᵢⱼ are obtained by fitting experimental VLE data; they are temperature dependent, often correlated with the van’t Hoff equation ln A = a + b/T. Examiners frequently ask to derive γ expressions from a given Gᴱ/RT form or to identify which model can represent azeotropy (Margules and van Laar can, Wilson cannot).

Temperature Dependence of Henry’s Constant and Gas Solubility Trends

Henry’s law constant K_H (in pressure‑over‑mole‑fraction form p = K_H x) is not truly constant; it varies with temperature according to the van’t Hoff relation d(ln K_H)/d(1/T) = –Δ_sol H°/R, where Δ_sol H° is the standard enthalpy of solution. For most gases Δ_sol H° is negative (exothermic dissolution), so K_H increases with temperature and solubility decreases — the familiar loss of carbonation in warm soda. Typical values: at 298 K, K_H(O₂) ≈ 4.4 × 10⁴ atm, K_H(N₂) ≈ 8.6 × 10⁴ atm, K_H(CO₂) ≈ 2.9 × 10³ atm. The temperature coefficient can be expressed as ln(K_H₂/K_H₁) = –Δ_sol H°/R (1/T₂ – 1/T₁). For O₂, Δ_sol H° ≈ –12 kJ mol⁻¹, giving a ~2 % rise in K_H per kelvin near room temperature. In contrast, gases that react with the solvent (e.g., NH₃, HCl) show an apparent Henry constant that includes chemical equilibrium; their temperature dependence is governed by both physical solubility and reaction enthalpy. A common examiner twist is to provide K_H at two temperatures and ask for Δ_sol H° or to predict the solubility change in a heated river. Students must remember that the Henry constant expressed in concentration units (M/atm) has the opposite temperature trend because the conversion factor involves the solvent density, which also changes with temperature.

Examiner's trap
A question gives K_H for CO₂ as 3.3 × 10³ atm at 298 K and 4.5 × 10³ atm at 308 K. Calculate the standard enthalpy of solution Δ_sol H° (in kJ mol⁻¹) assuming the van’t Hoff relation holds.
Use ln(K₂/K₁) = –Δ_sol H°/R (1/T₂ – 1/T₁). ln(4.5×10³ / 3.3×10³) = ln(1.3636) = 0.310. 1/T₂ – 1/T₁ = 1/308 – 1/298 = –0.000109 K⁻¹. Rearranging: Δ_sol H° = –R × 0.310 / (–0.000109) = 8.314 × 0.310 / 0.000109 ≈ 23 600 J mol⁻¹ = 23.6 kJ mol⁻¹. The positive sign indicates endothermic dissolution, which is atypical for CO₂; the data set is deliberately inconsistent to test sign handling. The correct physical Δ_sol H° for CO₂ is about –19 kJ mol⁻¹, so the trap is recognising the sign error.
Exam‑day strategy
When a Henry‑law problem supplies two temperatures, write the van’t Hoff equation first, substitute the given K_H values, and solve for Δ_sol H°. Keep units consistent (R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹). Check the sign: a rise in K_H with temperature means Δ_sol H° > 0 (endothermic), which is rare for simple gases — flag such data as a possible trick.

Colligative Properties in Mixed‑Solvent Systems and the Role of Activity Coefficients

Standard colligative formulas (ΔT_b = i K_b m, ΔT_f = i K_f m, π = i M R T) assume an ideal dilute solution in a single solvent. In mixed solvents the effective molality of solute particles is replaced by the solute activity a₂ = γ₂ m₂ (or mole fraction x₂ γ₂). The boiling‑point elevation becomes ΔT_b = (R T_b² / Δ_vap H) ln a₂, where Δ_vap H is the molar enthalpy of vaporisation of the mixed solvent. For a binary solvent (1 and 3) the solvent activity a₁ = x₁ γ₁ appears in the vapour‑pressure lowering expression (p°₁ – p₁)/p°₁ = x₂ γ₂ / (x₁ γ₁ + x₂ γ₂). The ebullioscopic constant K_b for the mixture is not a simple weighted average; it must be derived from the temperature derivative of the solvent activity at the boiling point. Practical calculations often use the Pitzer or UNIFAC models to obtain γ₁, γ₂ for the solvent mixture at the composition of interest. A typical exam scenario: a 0.1 mol kg⁻¹ NaCl solution in a 70 % (mass) water / 30 % ethanol mixture. The student must (i) compute the mixed‑solvent boiling point from the pure‑component boiling points and the mixture’s vapour‑pressure curve, (ii) estimate γ_NaCl from an ionic‑strength model (e.g., Debye–Hückel extended), and (iii) apply ΔT_b = i K_b,eff m with K_b,eff = R T_b² / Δ_vap H_mix. Ignoring solvent non‑ideality leads to errors of 10–30 % in ΔT_b for such systems.

Quantitative Treatment of Complex‑Ion Formation on Sparingly Soluble Salts

When a sparingly soluble salt MₐX_b dissolves in a ligand L that forms a complex MLₙ, the overall solubility increases because the free metal ion concentration is lowered. For AgCl(s) + 2 NH₃ ⇌ [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ + Cl⁻, the equilibrium constant K = K_sp × β₂, where β₂ is the overall formation constant of the diamminesilver(I) complex (β₂ ≈ 1.6 × 10⁷ at 298 K). The solubility s in the presence of a fixed total ammonia concentration C_NH₃ is obtained from mass balances: [Ag⁺] + [Ag(NH₃)₂⁺] = s, [Cl⁻] = s, [NH₃] + 2[Ag(NH₃)₂⁺] = C_NH₃. Substituting [Ag(NH₃)₂⁺] = β₂ [Ag⁺][NH₃]² and K_sp = [Ag⁺][Cl⁻] = [Ag⁺] s gives a cubic equation in s. In the limit of large excess ligand (C_NH₃ ≫ s), [NH₃] ≈ C_NH₃ and s ≈ √(K_sp β₂) C_NH₃. For AgCl, √(K_sp β₂) ≈ √(1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ × 1.6 × 10⁷) ≈ 1.7 × 10⁻², so 0.1 M NH₃ yields s ≈ 1.7 × 10⁻³ M, a 10⁴‑fold increase over pure water. Examiners often ask to derive the solubility expression for a 1:1 salt with a 1:2 complex, or to compare the effect of a monodentate versus a bidentate ligand (different β values). A frequent trap is forgetting that the ligand concentration in the formation constant is the free ligand concentration, not the analytical concentration.

Osmotic Pressure Measurements for Polymer Molar Mass: Van’t Hoff to Flory‑Huggins

Osmotic pressure π = i M R T is the basis of membrane osmometry for determining number‑average molar mass M_n of polymers. For a polymer solution the van’t Hoff equation is expanded as a virial series: π / c = R T (1/M_n + A₂ c + A₃ c² + …), where c is mass concentration (g L⁻¹) and A₂ is the second virial coefficient reflecting polymer‑solvent interactions. In a θ‑solvent A₂ = 0 and a plot of π/c versus c extrapolates to 1/M_n at c → 0. In good solvents A₂ > 0, causing upward curvature; in poor solvents A₂ < 0, leading to downward curvature and possible phase separation. The Flory‑Huggins lattice theory gives A₂ = (1/2 – χ) V₁ / (M₀²), where χ is the polymer‑solvent interaction parameter, V₁ the molar volume of solvent, and M₀ the molar mass of a repeat unit. Typical values: for polystyrene in benzene at 298 K, χ ≈ 0.45, A₂ ≈ 1.2 × 10⁻⁴ mol mL g⁻². Modern osmometers measure π at several concentrations (10⁻⁴–10⁻² g mL⁻¹) and fit the virial equation to obtain M_n and A₂ simultaneously. A common exam question provides π/c data at three concentrations and asks for M_n by linear extrapolation, testing whether the student recognises the need to use the intercept, not the slope. Another trap is confusing number‑average M_n (from osmometry) with weight‑average M_w (from light scattering); the two are equal only for monodisperse polymers.

  • Assuming activity coefficients are unity in mixed‑solvent colligative calculations — they can deviate strongly, especially with ethanol‑water.
  • Using the analytical ligand concentration instead of the free ligand concentration when applying formation constants to solubility problems.
  • Treating Henry’s constant as temperature‑independent; the van’t Hoff relation must be applied for any temperature change.
  • Confusing the Margules and Wilson models’ ability to predict liquid‑liquid equilibrium; Wilson cannot, Margules and van Laar can.
  • Extrapolating π/c versus c data without checking the sign of the second virial coefficient; a negative A₂ invalidates simple linear extrapolation.
  • Equating number‑average molar mass from osmometry with weight‑average molar mass from light scattering for polydisperse polymers.
  • Neglecting the temperature dependence of the ebullioscopic constant K_b when the solvent composition changes with temperature.
